( credit : WISAM HASHLAMOUN/FLASH90 ) <h> Settlement jurisdiction orders reshape administrative boundaries <p> Jurisdiction orders are decrees issued by the IDF designating areas in the West Bank as part of an Israeli settlement and reserving the development and control of the land for Israeli hands . <p> Unlike the construction of individual housing units , these orders redefine the administrative boundaries of settlements , creating the legal framework for future expansion before building begins . <p> " They settlement jurisdiction areas are ' legal ' land grabs that happen without any public debate , court oversight , or Palestinian recourse , " the analysis from Bimkom read . <p> Once a piece of land is designated as a settlement 's jurisdiction , it is allocated solely to future Israeli development . <p> Jurisdiction orders are the first step in expanding Israeli settlements in the West Bank because they determine which authority controls the land and who is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ settlement 's municipal jurisdiction is generally unavailable for Palestinian development , farming , or construction , even where no immediate building projects are planned . <p> According to a Bimkom analysis , the rapid increase in these orders reflects a shift in how settlement expansion is carried out . <p> Rather than relying exclusively on the approval of new housing projects , Israeli authorities have increasingly focused on expanding the territorial footprint of settlements through administrative decisions that receive comparatively little public attention . <p> The study found that many of the jurisdiction changes involved extending the boundaries of existing settlements , while others formalized new settlement outposts that had previously existed without official recognition . <p> In several cases , jurisdiction areas were also divided or reorganized , allowing separate settlements to be established under distinct municipal administrations . <p> By extending municipal boundaries and placing additional land under settlement jurisdiction , the orders create the legal and planning conditions for future infrastructure , residential neighborhoods , industrial zones , and roads connecting settlements across the West Bank , Bimkom argued . <p> The organization said the pace of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from previous years . <p> Because jurisdiction orders are signed by the military commander rather than debated in a public legislative process , they allow substantial territorial changes to occur with limited transparency and few opportunities for Palestinian communities to challenge the decisions , according to Bimkom 's analysis .

They remain real , and in some cases profound . They see settlement expansion , permanent occupation , and the denial of political rights to millions of Palestinians as incompatible with both democratic principles and Jewish ethics . They are horrified both by Hamas 's Oct. 7 , 2023 , massacre and by the devastating toll of war on innocent Palestinian civilians . <p> Our Jewish values require moral consistency , however , and an approach to Israel advocacy that asserts we have no right to question the country 's policies does not meet this moment . <p> Younger American Jews will not sustain a meaningful relationship with Israel if they are told they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> While most American Jews still believe the United States should help Israel address real security threats , polling shows they want that support to be strategic and accountable , not unconditional or open-ended.The two of us also believe true friendship requires mutual respect and accountability . <p> American aid and weapons must be used in accordance with American law and international standards . @@138689273 <h> Canada 's Jew-hatred problem <p> In Focus delivers deeper coverage of the political , cultural , and ideological issues shaping America . Published daily by senior writers and experts , these in-depth pieces go beyond the headlines to give readers the full picture . You can find our full list of In Focus pieces here . <h> Recommended Stories <p> In June , Dr. Emmanuel Moss , chief of cardiac surgery at the Jewish General Hospital in Montreal , announced that he was leaving Canada for the United States . A Canadian doing this is n't normally newsworthy . Many upwardly-minded Canucks have taken their talents to America . Yet the thing about Dr. Moss is that he 's Jewish at a time when his people are increasingly unwelcome in the Great White North . " The rise of antisemitism in Montreal " compelled him to leave , Dr. Moss wrote in a letter explaining his decision . <p> Advertisement <p> Moss is one of a growing number of Canadian Jews who are packing their bags . Others include Gad Saad , a popular social commentator and author of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ University of Mississippi . The sorry truth is that many Canadian Jews see no future for themselves in their home and native land . This should be a cautionary tale for other countries , not least the U.S. <p> Canada has the fourth-largest Jewish population on earth ( some 400,000 people ) , trailing only Israel , the U.S. , and France . Its Jews once thrived . Their story approximated that of American Jews . Many had fled the antisemitism of Eastern Europe for greener pastures on this side of the Atlantic . Accorded freedom and equality in Canada , they made significant contributions in medicine , law , education , the arts , and other fields . The community 's most prominent members include musician Leonard Cohen , journalist Morley Safer , and actor William Shatner . Jews were proud to be Canadians , and other Canadians were proud to call Jews their compatriots . <p> Jew-hatred killed that modus vivendi . By some measures , Canada has become one of the most antisemitic countries on earth . Just look at the data . <p> Advertisement <p> Last @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ In other words , there is roughly one antisemitic incident per 59 Jews . Compare that to the U.S. , where the ratio is one antisemitic incident per 1,116 Jews -- the American Jewish population is approximately 7 million people , and there were 6,274 antisemitic incidents in the U.S. last year . That means Canada experiences around 19 times as many antisemitic incidents as the U.S. on a per capita basis . For all the talk about surging antisemitism in the United States , the situation is far graver in Canada . <p> Antisemites have targeted synagogues and Jewish schools with alacrity . In June , Toronto 's police chief told the press that youth were being recruited to carry out attacks on Jewish institutions around the city . " It is clear that some of the people hiring these criminals want to create a sense of fear in our communities , including in the Jewish community , " he said . <p> Toronto 's Jewish community , which accounts for roughly half all Canadian Jews , has been fearful for some time . In June 2026 , there was an attempted arson attack on Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom , a Reform congregation in Westmount . In November 2023 , Montreal 's Yeshiva Gedola , a school for young men , was targeted by gunfire two times in one week . In May 2024 , the entryway of Vancouver 's Schara Tzedeck synagogue was set on fire . Since the October 7 attacks and the ensuing war in Gaza , Jewish students have been harassed for simply being Jewish . As in other rich countries , activists professing to oppose " Zionists " invariably target Jews . Calls for " intifada , " meaning the death of Jews , have been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hosted by Jewish students . All of this was unthinkable in Canada just a few years ago . <p> As is the case in Western Europe , mass migration explains a great deal of Canada 's new antisemitism . The policies of former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau encouraged millions to come to Canada , where immigrants now comprise 23% of the population , compared to 15% in the United States . Although many of these newcomers are n't antisemitic , many are , and some put their hatred of Jews into action . <p> Advertisement <p> Canadian authorities have thwarted several terror plots by migrants against Jews . @@138744477 <h> American campuses are being bought by foreign actors - opinion <h> Foreign money is reshaping American higher education , raising urgent questions about influence , ideology , and the battle for the next generation 's beliefs . <p> Follow us on GoogleStudent protesters stand watch along the perimeter of an encampment supporting Palestinians at the Columbia University campus , during the ongoing conflict between Israel and the Palestinian Islamist group Hamas , in New York City , U.S. , April 25 , 2024 ( photo credit : REUTERS/Caitlin Ochs ) ByHARRY ZIMMERMAN JULY 5 , 2026 18:12Updated : JULY 5 , 2026 18:14 <p> Americans are focused on the wrong war because Iran is not the most dangerous battlefield . Victories in conventional war are quantitative and can be measured . The real war is much more insidious , as it is a war about winning the hearts and minds of a new generation , and that war is being fought with dollars , not bullets . <h> Conquering minds , not territory <p> A military war has a beginning , a middle , and an end . Bombs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ eventually stop fighting , and relationships are rehabilitated . The destruction is horrifying , but it is visible because it has a location that can be photographed , measured , cleared away , and rebuilt . Much of Europe lay in ruins after World War II . Yet today , its cities thrive because steel , concrete , and glass can always be rebuilt . <p> But ideas are different . <p> History 's greatest tyrants understood that a lasting victory comes from conquering minds , not land . Hitler did not rely on military power alone - he invested enormous effort and dollars in propaganda , education , film , radio , newspapers , and mass rallies because he understood that if you could redefine and reset what people accepted as normal , morality could be rewritten . The Soviet Communist Party reshaped generations through schools and state-controlled media . Mao Zedong launched the Cultural Revolution not simply to control the government , but to transform an entire culture 's values , history , and identity . More recently , ISIS devoted enormous resources to digital propaganda because they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> The foreign actors funding American education <p> That is why Americans should pay close attention to foreign funding of our educational institutions . According to data compiled by the US Department of Education under Section 117 of the Higher Education Act , American universities reported receiving more than $50 billion in foreign gifts and contracts between 1986 and 2020 , with a significant surge in disclosures after the 2019 enforcement actions . <p> A 2020 report by the National Association of Scholars estimates that the true total may exceed $100 billion because of underreporting . Qatar has consistently ranked among the largest foreign sources of that funding , contributing more than $4.7 billion to US universities between 2001 and 2021 , according to Department of Education data and analyses by the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy ( ISGAP ) . Universities have welcomed these funds and even solicited foreign entities to support research , facilities , scholarships , and academic programs . <p> But money is never just money because every significant investment carries with it the seduction of influence . It would be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a foreign government spends billions of dollars helping educate America 's future leaders , one must ask what return it expects . This is not warfare with missiles or fighter jets ; it is influence exercised through the filtering of ideas , and the manipulation of historical narrative through culture and education . If military conflict seeks to conquer territory , ideological influence seeks to conquer the way people think . <p> That is why this battlefield is so dangerous . It is not fought over the Strait of Hormuz , but in New York , California , Kentucky , Texas , and every other state where tomorrow 's voters are being educated today . It has often been said that votes are to a democracy what bullets are to a revolution . Influence a generation of voters , and you change the democracy in which we live . Once ideas and influence break out of their embryonic state , they become rooted and more difficult to reverse . <h> The Cash Behind the Encampments <p> I witnessed something that brought this point home to me . During the Gaza @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . There were hundreds of tents and what struck me was how similar they all were . Unless you believe there happened to be a giant sale on that particular tent , it was obvious that this was not a spontaneous event . It was organized and well-funded . That observation does not necessarily tell us who supplied the tents or who financed the encampment , but it raises a broader question that deserves scrutiny : who is organizing , funding , and supporting these movements on American campuses , and what ideology are they advancing ? Is it simply an expression of free speech , or is it an attempt to manipulate the way people think , finding cover behind our Constitution to gain entrance and then tear our democracy apart from the inside ? <p> The greatest victories are often won before a single shot is fired - when a society 's understanding of truth , morality , and loyalty quietly shifts until the change feels natural . Once that happens , bombs become almost unnecessary because the battlefield has already moved into the minds of the next @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ territory - it 's about conquering the future . If we ignore it , we are essentially surrendering . <p> The author is an entrepreneur , former Executive Director of the Clinton Foundation , retired airline pilot , and a current member of the Congressional Medal of Honor leadership board of directors . <p> This op-ed is published in partnership with a coalition of organizations that fight antisemitism across the world . The final act , " Right of Return , " marks a sadder occasion , in 2024 . Between the acts , a screen displays an ingeniously calibrated cascade of digital interactions : initially , Yahoo and " . edu " e-mails ; then a Facebook group , BirthLeft ; and gradually -- as the political landscape tilts ominously -- a WhatsApp group . There 's a sensual specificity to the staging , from the Proustian sight of a teal-butted 2001 iMac to the sounds of news junkies snarking about Thomas Friedman or trading in-jokes about the shrimp at an Israeli wedding . <p> And yet a bratty skepticism welled up in me as the play unfolded . Clashes flared only to be tamped out ; repercussions were softened , often comedically , as an outsider crashed the debate . Lines were uncrossed . Plays , like people , have value systems . I share the ones central to " Birthright " : talking across divides , keeping the conversation going . I , too , am frustrated by the online reflex to sneer . But those ideals block the play from being fully honest -- by letting ugliness stick around . " Birthright " culminates in a fiery showdown in Act III , when the left-wing Izzy and the liberal Chaya wield phones like knives , competitively Googling " Theodor Herzl colonialism " and " 1930s partition plan Israel " as Noah struggles to talk them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; I usually mean this as an insult , but in Spector 's case it 's not all bad . Everyone -- including Alona , the only one who 's lived in Israel -- gets to make their case in full , just as the anti-vaxxers did in " Eureka Day . " But is it enough to hear people out ? To retreat to " It 's complicated " ? <p> I kept sensing the elisions . We hear about MAGA Zionists -- Fox News-watching fathers , Tel Aviv neighbors -- but they 're all offstage . By design , this is a play about a narrow slice of Ashkenazic Jews , college-educated members of Conservative shuls . ( This is n't a political category ; it 's the middle of the continuum of Reform , Conservative , and Orthodox , or , as the joke goes , " lazy , hazy , and crazy . " ) It 's a play about two-state Zionists resistant to the term " genocide " and anti-Zionists pushing them to use it , a demographic just left of the women from the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ TV show " Crazy Ex-Girlfriend , " who spar over their anti-racist bona fides , then add , politely , " Though of course I support Israel . " Yet " Birthright , " despite having been written , daringly , into the current crisis , feels one step behind . <p> Or perhaps the problem is that it 's too short ! This may be the first time I 've thought a play might work better as a television series , with space for its characters to grow . As it happens , there is a series like that : " Long Story Short , " an emotionally chewy animated Netflix series by Raphael Bob-Waksberg , the creator of " BoJack Horseman . " A portrait of the Schwoopers , a liberal Jewish family in the Bay Area , " Long Story Short , " like " Birthright , " jumps across decades , allowing for a prismatic portrayal of Jewish identity , in all its pride and ambivalence . Nobody mentions Israel , which is , I guess , a cop-out -- but also a magic trick that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The standout episode -- the conversion history of Kendra , a Black striver married to the Schwoopers ' daughter , Shira -- sticks its landing , enabling the viewer to see faith as a refuge , not a cage . <p> Then , there 's " Giant , " the other big new play to address Jewish identity . It has a different sort of peculiar timing : the script was completed the week before October 7th , a tragedy that imbues it with an unwieldy resonance . Swashbuckling and polemical , " Giant " is set in 1983 , on the afternoon that Roald Dahl gave a radio interview making plain the links between his anti-Israel punditry and his private antisemitism . An old-fashioned ideas play , it has its contrivances . But its ability to tolerate discomfort is its strength , particularly through its most original figure -- Dahl 's friend and publisher Tom Maschler , deftly portrayed by Elliot Levey . A secular Jew and a Holocaust survivor , Tom is a cool customer : a louche , assimilated Brit whose astringent view of his ethnicity , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all , ultimately leaves him more vulnerable , not less -- hamstrung by his intimacy with a brilliant bigot . The contradictions of their closeness are n't papered over ; the unease is allowed to linger , inflamed and ineradicable . <p> " Birthright " works under different rules : it ca n't subtract Israel , like " Long Story Short , " or take refuge in the past , like " Giant . " But , as heartfelt and skillfully performed as " Birthright " is , in its eagerness to become a healing ritual for the audience it dodges what Dahl , in an acid exchange in " Giant , " deems " the vexing bit . " In Act I , Lev is thrilled by a Talmudic concept : that letting contradictory interpretations coexist is a distinctly Jewish way of encountering Hashem , or God . That 's a beautiful idea , but in drama it can feel like throwing up one 's hands . @@138910169 <p> Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani , the former emir of Qatar who transformed the small Gulf state into one of the world 's wealthiest and most influential nations , has died . He was 74 . <p> A charismatic figure with a friendly demeanour , the father emir assumed the reins of power in 1995 . Regarded as the architect of modern Qatar , he embarked on leading development and reform plans and education programmes using his country 's vast natural gas wealth to push an ambitious agenda of political , economic and social reforms . <p> During his reign , Qatar 's gross domestic product ( GDP ) increased more than 24-fold , while production from the North Field turned the country into the world 's largest exporter of liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) by 2006 . In record time , the small nation 's LNG production capacity reached 77 million tonnes per annum , according to government figures . <p> His tenure also saw the establishment of the Qatar Foundation , the launch of the Al Jazeera news channel in 1996 , the promulgation of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of municipal elections in which women were granted the right to vote and stand as candidates . Under his leadership , the Gulf nation secured the right to host the 2022 FIFA World Cup , the first time an Arab country had done so . <p> Born in Doha in January 1952 , Sheikh Hamad graduated from the British Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst before becoming commander of Qatar 's armed forces . He became heir apparent and defence minister in 1977 , assumed power as emir on June 27 , 1995 , and handed over leadership to his heir apparent , Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani , on June 25 , 2013 . <p> Advertisement <p> The peaceful , voluntary transfer of leadership was rare in the region . <p> " The future lies ahead of you , the children of this homeland , as you usher into a new era where young leadership hoists the banner , " Sheikh Hamad said as he announced his abdication and the carefully crafted transition to Sheikh Tamim , who was then 33 . <p> Sheikh Hamad had wide-ranging visions for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years , its mediation was brought to bear on the conflict in Sudan 's Darfur region , Lebanese factional feuding and the rift between the Palestinian groups Hamas and Fatah . <p> Before Sheikh Hamad 's abdication , Qatar formally opened an office for the Taliban at the request of the United States , which set the stage for talks between Washington and the Afghan group that ultimately led to NATO and the US 's chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 . <p> During his rule , Qatar was among the few countries to side with the popular uprisings that became known as the Arab Spring . <p> In Egypt , Al Jazeera defied a broadcast ban showing the world antigovernment and pro-democracy protests . In Syria , Sheikh Hamad initially tried to convince then-President Bashar al-Assad to step down in the face of mass antigovernment protests , before Doha severed ties with Damascus over demonstrators ' killings by government forces . In Libya , Qatar went further by supporting a NATO military mission that ultimately led to the overthrow of long-term ruler Muammer Gaddafi . <p> But the cause @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fitting perhaps that one of his last official visits was when he became the first head of state to go to the Gaza Strip in more than a decade . @@138996977 <h> Echoes of Karbala , Iran beyond the shadows of war <h> The Iran that exists beyond stereotypes and western media headlines is a land of faith , resilience , culture , and quiet human dignity <p> ' There lives a beautiful , ancient society determined to preserve its dignity , its culture , and its humanity , even in the darkest of times ' Photo Credit : AFP <p> Finally , the cat is out of the bag . With United States President Donald Trump first announcing a 20% surcharge for facilitating the passage of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , and now shifting the focus to investments in America ( " Trade and Investment Deals that the various Gulf States will be making into the United States " ) , the " art of the deal " has been laid bare . The war with Iran was never about democracy , human rights , or non-proliferation ; those are merely pretexts to control Iran 's vast energy reserves and the strategic choke points of global trade . But behind the sterile headlines of geopolitics lies a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ personal : my experience of stepping into Iran at one of the most extraordinary , painful moments in its modern history . <p> Late in the evening on July 1 , I was deeply moved and , frankly , astonished , to receive an invitation , extended on behalf of the Rehbar , Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei , to attend the funeral ceremonies of his father , the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei . The invitation came suddenly ; everything -- from the visa and booking the flights to arranging the state protocols -- moved with breathless speed . My eldest daughter , Irtiqa , was gripped by fear when she heard the news . Aware of my outspoken stance on Gaza and concerned about the dangers of travelling to Iran , she only calmed down after extracting a promise from me that I would return as soon as the ceremonies were over . Within hours , I was aboard a Mahan Air flight bound for Tehran . <h> The real Iran <p> Landing in Tehran , I braced myself for an atmosphere thick with fear and wartime paralysis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , composed calm . The officials who received us were polite , orderly , and reassuring . The airport 's VIP lounge bustled with diplomats and leaders from across the globe . Former Union Minister Salman Khurshid and several distinguished spiritual leaders from India were on my flight . It gradually dawned on me that I was the only female political leader invited from India , and a Sunni woman at that . In a region so often fractured by sectarian divides , this gesture of inclusive solidarity made the honour all the more profound . <p> From the airport to our hotel , the meticulous organisation was striking . There was no chaos , no frantic mobilisation . No one looking at the quiet , efficient streets would have believed that this was a country living under the constant threat of annihilation . Upon reaching the hotel , after being warmly welcomed , a young Iranian woman in a flowing black abaya was assigned to guide me , attending to my every need with effortless grace . <p> But what shattered my preconceptions most was the sheer presence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I saw female journalists , broadcasters , and camera operators , clad in abayas and headscarves , interviewing international delegates with fierce professional confidence . I have long known of Iran 's high female literacy rates and the prominence of women in universities , medicine , and education . Yet , seeing them command the media landscape stood in stark , defiant contrast to the western caricature of the silent , secluded Iranian woman . <h> A grief beyond words <p> The next day remains permanently etched in my soul . @@139193571 <h> India must lead in securing the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb <h> New Delhi 's leadership can help prevent another major shipping crisis in the Red Sea <p> ' This time around , the situation is more unpredictable ' Photo Credit : Getty Images/iStockphoto <p> On the heels of the Strait of Hormuz crisis comes the new threat -- a Strait of Bab el-Mandeb crisis . On July 16 , Reuters reported that Iran had instructed the Houthis to close the Strait ( which is between Yemen and the Horn of Africa ) if the United States attacked Iran 's power plants . <p> Whether the Houthis have the capacity to threaten the Strait or whether this is part of Iran 's signalling to the U.S. is secondary . What is important is that this represents a risk to one-third of India 's entire trade . <h> Revisiting 2024 <p> We have been here before . When the Gaza war started in October 2023 , the Ansarallah group in Yemen , also known as the Houthis , claimed solidarity with the Palestinians and launched drones and missiles at Israel . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at least 40 vessels in the Red Sea , claiming that the vessels were linked to or bound for Israel . <p> In response , the U.S. , together with allies including Singapore and Sri Lanka , launched Operation Prosperity Guardian ( December 2023 ) to ensure " freedom of navigation " in the Red Sea . This was followed by United Nations Security Council Resolution 2722 ( 2024 ) . which was adopted in January 2024 . Israel also carried out unilateral strikes against the Houthis . The Indian Navy rescued the crew of a British tanker after it was set on fire ( January 26-27 , 2024 ) . By the time the U.S declared a ceasefire in May 2025 , the Houthis had been weakened , but much of the damage had already been done . <p> Marine insurance companies tend to be highly risk-averse . With over 90% of the world 's shipping insured by just 12 protection and indemnity ( P&amp;I ) clubs , shipowners have limited room to negotiate . Between November 2023 and March 2024 , at least 2,000 ships avoided the Suez @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This delayed critical imports to India . Global shipping routes effectively reverted to what was being done 170 years ago . Egypt lost a quarter of the Suez Canal 's revenue . By July 2024 , Israel 's Red Sea port of Eilat had filed for bankruptcy . <p> This time around , the situation is more unpredictable . With U.S. forces in the region focused on Iran , it is unclear whether they will seek to secure the Red Sea as they did before . <p> Even in 2024 , when India-bound ships were attacked by the Houthis , New Delhi had to lean directly on Tehran to bring the attacks to a halt . But that was a different time for India-Iran ties . Meanwhile , the UN Security Council is more divided today than ever before , and even if it manages to call for " freedom of navigation " in the Red Sea , it is unlikely to pass a resolution approving a force to implement that call . China is also likely to again take a unilateral approach to protecting its shipping in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> If the Houthis resume attacks on shipping in the Strait , the impact on India 's economy -- which is already reeling from the Strait of Hormuz crisis -- would be dire . While India has now ordered that no Indian mariner be deployed on ships bound to or from the Strait of Hormuz , extending the same restriction to a busy route such as the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb would not be easy and would adversely affect the safety and welfare of thousands of Indian seafarers . <h> What India should do <p> In 2024 , France stayed out of a U.S.-led operation to guard its role in mediating between Hezbollah and Israel in Lebanon . They had refused to join the alliance against the Houthis in 2024 , given their own stance on Gaza . This time , with their economies at stake , they may not stand by . On July 20 , the Houthis announced a " maritime embargo " on Saudi ships , seen as a threat against their transit through the Bab el-Mandeb . @@139209177 <h> A Teen Reporter Searched for His Community in the Epstein Files . Adults Freaked Out <p> An Instagram post turned one California student newspaper into a free-speech flash point . The students say they were just doing their homework . <p> Ben Mueller.PHOTOGRAPH : AMY HARRITY <p> Ben Mueller 's assignment for his journalism class was to tell a news story -- any news story -- in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow . So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10 , 2026 , he grabbed a snack , went upstairs to his room , and settled in to work . <p> After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination -- scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth -- Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice 's Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older ( he was , just barely ) . Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier . <p> Mueller really liked working in his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strolling and biking along one of Marin County , California 's sun-dappled waterways . Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America , Mueller could n't help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein . " I think it 's very difficult to get an immense amount of money without -- this is my opinion -- without doing something a little shady , " Mueller says . So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin . <p> He found thousands . Most of them were trivial ( Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware , headquartered in nearby Corte Madera ) . " Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned . Last Friday , President Trump announced his latest tariffs to go into effect . He targeted 60 economies . I say " 60 economies , " because one of the 60 targeted was Taiwan , which is not regarded by the United States as a country but only as an economy . So , 60 economies including Taiwan ; 59 countries plus Taiwan . <p> The ostensible basis of this new round of tariff increases was to combat forced labor . President Trump used a provision in American law that allows the president power to impose tariffs on countries that use forced or slave labor , and he said : That 's it . In order to fight forced or slave labor , these 60 economies , including Taiwan , are going to be targeted by a new round of tariff increases . <p> The grounds given for the tariffs are not really very plausible . There is no or barely any factual showing that all of these 60 were engaged in some way in forced labor . The United States , after all , is not completely clean on this question either , and there 's no graduation of the tariff to the alleged cause . The United States economy is open in many ways to forced labor . <p> Pretty obviously , what is going on here is that Trump is looking for some legal basis to reinstate the tariffs that he has had struck down in the past . President Trump originally used an emergency economic authority from the 1970s . The Supreme Court told him he could n't do it . Then he fell back on a temporary provision that allowed him to impose tariffs for a period of time , I think 150 days , and that time has run out . So now he 's looking for what he can get . <p> As the president returns again and again and again to imposing tariffs on the world , a question has to be asked : What on earth could any Trump supporter imagine the president is possibly doing that is , in any way , in the American national interest ? The emotional basis , the argumentative basis , the intellectual basis for tariffs is that we are supposedly reindustrializing the United States . But since Donald Trump has become president , manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined by the tens of thousands , probably somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 net manufacturing jobs fewer as I record in the summer of 2026 than when Donald Trump became president at the beginning of 2025 . <p> Because other sectors other employment sectors are continuing to grow , especially health care , this loss of a net 100,000 manufacturing jobs means that manufacturing as a share of nonfarm payrolls has now dipped below 8 percent , which is the lowest level that manufacturing has had in American employment since figures began . Maybe it was lower in 1776 than it is now , but since good figures began , this is the lowest . It 's a record . So obviously , it 's not working . And it 's not just jobs that are being lost . Manufacturing output and manufacturing investment also seem to be in decline . This is a little harder to calculate because there 's a huge capital-investment boom going on because of artificial-intelligence data centers . A lot of money is being committed to these data centers , and the question is : To what extent does this get counted as manufacturing investment and whatnot ? But private economists who have tried to separate out seem to be in some kind of agreement that , at best , manufacturing investment is flat in the Trump year and a half , maybe down a little bit , because of the problem of the Trump tariffs . <p> The thing I wish I could pound into the head of tariff supporters is that every tariffed item is not only a product that you sell to consumers ; it 's also an input into something else . When you impose tariffs on goods , you make not just things more expensive for American consumers -- you make things more expensive for the American companies that buy those things and put them into other things . It 's a house-that-Jack-built problem . Every time you make an input more expensive , you make the ultimate product more expensive and make the final American product that much less competitive on world markets . And the result is : You ca n't compete , so you sell less , so you invest less , so you employ less . <p> A large part of the attraction of tariffs to Donald Trump seems to be that they appeal to his desire for dominance . His perception of the world is divided into subjects and into enemies , and if you 're not a subject , then you 're an enemy . And if you 're an enemy , then there are no rules . And if you 're a subject , for that matter , there are n't any rules either . That everything is an expression of will and ego , and all economics is a matter of I win , you lose , and if I do n't feel I 'm winning , then I must be losing . <p> This has become the signature political and economic philosophy of an entire political party under Donald Trump . The party that used to stand for markets and enterprise , the Republican Party , the party of Reagan and Romney . We 're on a bad track here , and these latest tariffs mark another bad milestone on that bad track . We need to get off this , and we need to start creating in freedom and with rules . <p> That does n't mean that we pretend that China is not a problem . China is a problem , and there 's forced labor in China . And China is a rule-breaker and steals intellectual property . You need a China-specific solution to the problem of trade , not a solution that destroys the whole apparatus of trade with all of America 's friends and , increasingly , former friends . <p> The United States is now bound in a grinding and frustrating war with Iran . It needs all the friends it can get . The idea that it is waging economic aggression on all of its partners and then acting baffled and befuddled that these partners do n't help out on the Iran problem -- a war that the United States started and that it did not have to start and that now it ca n't get out of -- that just , again , seems to be another bad milestone on another bad path . <p> The way out of all of America 's problems -- it 's not the whole solution , but it 's the beginning of a solution -- is to return to the path of free and fair trade with friendly-minded nations , bracketing China as a special problem , and otherwise dropping tariffs to the lowest rates possible and returning to the days when the United States negotiated agreements with its friends to trade in freedom and prosperity with mutual benefit and understanding that true trade makes all those who participate in it better off . <p> And now my dialogue with Jonathan Chait . <p> Music <p> Frum : Jonathan Chait has dedicated 30 years as one of this country 's sharpest , wittiest , and most ornery advocates for liberalism , first at The New Republic , then at New York magazine , and since 2024 at The Atlantic . As I mentioned at the top of the program , my book this week is a work of history -- 1177 BC : The Year Civilization Collapsed , by Eric Cline . Published in 2014 by Princeton University Press . <p> Now , I have not yet seen The Odyssey . I may be alone on my block . It sounds wonderful , and I 'm keen to get to it . But one of the things that I am remarking with admiration is that as people have gone to see The Odyssey , they have become fascinated by this question of the transition from one period of civilization to another . A character , I think it 's Odysseus himself , says in the movie , " Our age of bronze is collapsing . " Which is maybe a little on the nose for movie dialogue , but is right . <p> The Odyssey is a story set in the Bronze Age , written in the Iron Age , measured by which metal was the predominant metal that went into weapons of war and other kinds of tools . And there was a big collapse in between the two . And Eric Cline 's book 1177 : The Year Civilization Collapsed is a study of the collapse and an attempt to explain why it happened . <p> As I understand , and again , I have n't seen the movie , but the great theme of Christopher Nolan 's Odyssey is that this collapse is , first and foremost , a moral collapse . One civilization has had the kind of life energy seep out of it and is giving way to a new and successor civilization that will be guided by different rules and different values . <p> And indeed , there really was , across the eastern Mediterranean , a remarkable collapse around the year 1177 B.C. The Hittite Empire -- which was the superpower of the time based in what is now southern Turkey -- that vanished entirely , and its capital disappeared . Across the Mediterranean , city-states vanished . The Minoan civilization vanished . The New Kingdom in Egypt did n't quite vanish , but it lost a lot of its military power and never again exerted the kind of power over the region that it had before about the year 1200 . Mycenaean Greece , which is where the the characters in The Iliad and The Odyssey supposedly come from , that civilization utterly collapsed . It even lost the ability to read and to write for hundreds of years , only to reemerge later as an Iron Age civilization . And so it is , through up and down the Levant , into the islands , Cyprus . <p> So what happened ? Eric Cline tries to give us an answer . But the key thing to keep in mind , as to the background that enabled all this is that bronze , which is the weapon that the heroes of The Iliad and The Odyssey used for , the metal that they used for their weapons . And that was the main form of armor and tools . <p> Bronze is a compound of copper and tin . So copper was relatively abundant in the Mediterranean world . There were copper mines in Cyprus and in other places . But tin was scarce in that part of the world and had to be brought to be united with the copper from very far-flung places -- as far as Cornwall in Great Britain and Afghanistan in the center of Asia . <p> So when you 're committed to bronze , you 're committed to very global trade routes . And because the trade routes are so extended , you build large states . Because you have large states , you need ways to manage the states , including organized religion and reading and writing and some kind of numbering system . How do you keep track of how much tin has moved from Afghanistan to Babylonia , and when it moved , and who moved it ? You need some form of writing . And you need a bureaucracy . You need comparably sophisticated and elaborated states . <p> Something happened around the year 1177 B.C.E. , and Cline makes a good case that it 's a compound of ecological effects . Droughts and earthquakes that weakened the states , ended their ability to import tin , reduced the availability of the bronze alloy made from copper and tin , and set these states reeling backward and made them militarily vulnerable to invaders and small bands that otherwise they would 've just brushed off with superior strength . <p> Through the Bronze Age , people knew about iron . But iron was a more difficult material to work . In particular , it required a lot of heat . And it just seemed that bronze -- which was easier to work with and had a lot of prestige attached to it -- that that was the natural metal of choice . But once the bronze is no longer available because the tin has become hard to get , people are forced back to figure out ways to work with the iron . And once they do so , they find that iron is a dramatically superior weapon of war . Makes sharper , stronger swords , spears , and arrowheads . And so iron replaces it , and the world never looks backward to bronze . Bronze is from then on used primarily for statuary and art , because it remains a prestige material , but it 's not a workable material . <p> But the Cline story is one of environmental change leading to material innovation , not a story of moral decay . It was n't that people somehow lost faith in themselves and therefore turned away from bronze , and then found a new faith and therefore turned to iron . They had very practical problems . Now , I do n't want to dispute the importance to art of telling stories about moral decay and moral regeneration . But as we 're trying to understand why civilizations actually change , I mean , morality surely plays a part in it . Anyone watching the crisis of American democracy right now has to face that the greatness of a society and the ebb of greatness can be attributed to moral defects in that society . <p> But we also need to pay a lot of attention to ecological changes that force change upon society , and to the material responses to environmental change . Because while we 're not doing a great job in 21st-century America to adapting to our moral challenges , we 're doing an even worse job of adapting to climate changes . And if climate is what felled the Hittites , and as other historians will tell us , if climate is what felled the Romans , and if climate is what , as other historians again tell , felled the Ming Empire and led to the rise of new civilizations in China -- then climate , if we do n't pay attention to it , it could be the falling of us . <p> So as we enjoy the movie , as we absorb its powerful moral lessons , we also need to keep our eye on the material world , the world of climate and weather . Maybe we ca n't control it , but we 'd best learn to adapt to it . Because if we do n't , it will be the end of us . <p> Thanks so much for watching The David Frum Show this week .
